EXCLUSIVE: Patchway Studios, the UK studio facility that supported Season 2 of Disney’s Rivals and Netflix hit A Good Girl’s Guide To Murder, is attempting to fend off a closure threat levelled by one of its own investors.
The Bristol-based operation is the subject of a winding up petition from angel investor Annabel Schild, who is arguing that she is owed around £100,000 ($135,000).
In the UK, a winding up petition is often the last resort taken by a creditor when attempting to recover debt. It can put a business into liquidation, potentially imperilling its operations.
Schild’s claim against Patchway Studios, trading as Camera Studios (Patchway) Ltd, was before the business division of the High Court earlier this month. Judge Agnello KC adjourned the hearing to a later date.
In a statement to Deadline, Schild’s attorney said she had “little other option” but to pursue the petition because payment has been due for a “significant amount of time.”
Watch on Deadline
Patchway said the issues will be “resolved in due course.” The company’s position is that all other investors have agreed to reschedule their loans, and Schild has been paid her returns in recent years.
In Schild’s telling, she issued a loan to Patchway in 2022 and repayment was due in May 2024, but Patchway recently “confirmed it was not in a position to pay anything, not even interest that was due.”
Her lawyer continued: “Ms Schild did not take these steps lightly and had sought engagement with the company before pursuing legal action. Regrettably, no proposal of any substance towards repayment was made, leaving Ms Schild with no choice but to take formal action.”
The attorney added that Schild looks forward to Patchway “making good on promises” that all creditors will be repaid from “proposed fundraising activities.”
“She would be very pleased if all creditors are returned sums that they are owed so that the company can continue to trade, and hopes that the business does continue to operate in the future in a prudent manner for the benefit of all present and future creditors, stakeholders, interested parties and the wider community,” the statement read.
A Patchway spokesperson said: “As this is an ongoing legal process, we can’t go into any detail, but what I can say with confidence is that the issues raised by Ms Schild will be resolved in due course.”
Schild’s position is that her petition has the support of another creditor owed money. Patchway disputes the allegation that it is being chased for cash by another creditor.
Founded in August 2021, Patchway’s first major production was ITV/MGM+ series The Winter King. The studio facility has also hosted Paramount+ series The Crow Girl and supported Down Cemetery Road for Apple TV+. Patchway also has a facility in Battersea, London.

The Karnataka Legislature’s monsoon session will begin on August 13 with an ignominious first in recent history: a Cabinet with not even a symbolic representation of women.
The last fortnight has been marked by endless squabbles over Cabinet expansion and portfolio allocation, with intense arguments on ways to ensure caste and regional representation. Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar and party functionaries have made multiple trips to New Delhi to consult with the high command, and spent much energy trying to placate “powerful” leaders who are miffed over being denied Cabinet berths or over not getting what are described as “plum portfolios.”
However, women’s representation has clearly not been regarded as an issue worth breaking a sweat over. When asked by the media why not a single woman was included in his 33-member Cabinet, Mr. Shivakumar candidly admitted that there was “no urgency” in the matter, while casually assuring that the one vacant place would be filled by a woman. In fact, it was in an equally casual manner that Gayathri Shanthegowda, the lone woman who was in the Congress high command’s approved first list of Ministers, disappeared before the swearing-in ceremony, as the urgent demands of other powerful interest groups took over.
This situation is nothing short of ironic for two reasons: Congress has nationally been vociferously arguing for 33% women’s reservation, without encumbering it with delimitation or any other riders. At the State level, the Congress government has come to power riding on the back of five guarantees, two of which are specifically aimed at women’s empowerment. While the Gruha Lakshmi scheme promises ₹2,000 a month to women heads of eligible families, Shakti offers free travel to women in select buses.
Symbolic representation
The signalling is that while women are very crucial as voters, they are the last priority when it comes to sharing political power. The final electoral rolls published ahead of the 2023 elections showed that women voters outnumbered men in 17 electoral divisions out of the 34 in Karnataka. Naveddu Nilladiddare, a network of feminists and women’s rights groups, in a letter to the Chief Minister, put it succinctly: “An all-male Cabinet is not an oversight. It is a political choice. It sends an unmistakable message that women and women’s leadership remain dispensable when it comes to the exercise of state power.”
Interestingly, while there have been multiple street protests by supporters of leaders demanding their induction into Cabinet — foregrounding their caste, region, seniority etc. — there were hardly any protests against the non-inclusion of women in the Cabinet. There was some feeble noise in Belagavi in north Karnataka over Lakshmi Hebbalkar, who handled the Women and Child Development portfolio under the Siddaramaiah-led government, being dropped, but none on the larger question of women’s representation. Brahmins not being represented in the Cabinet grabbed more attention than women being denied a place.
The history of electoral politics in Karnataka shows that women’s share in political representation has always been abysmal, much like the rest of the country. In the 2023 Assembly elections, out of a total of 2,613 candidates, 185 were women. Of them, 10 were elected (with one more added in bypolls), which constitutes about 4.5% of the total Assembly strength. In the first two elections in Karnataka in 1957 and 1962, the share of women’s representation stood at 6.25% and 8.65%, respectively, the latter being the highest ever. Since then, the share has fluctuated, with the 1972 election seeing not even a single woman elected to the Assembly out of the 28 who contested. This is all the more striking in a State which was a pioneer in giving 50% reservation to women in local bodies.
The representation of women in Ministry too has been symbolic across parties, with the highest being four when the late S.M. Krishna was the Chief Minister. Women are often given what are regarded as “light weight” portfolios such as Women and Child Development or Kannada and Culture.
No doubt Mr. Shivakumar will stick to his promise of filling the one vacant berth with a woman, but that will not go beyond what it has always been — a symbolic gesture — in the absence of a system that makes representation count.

Nihang in 60s, worked as 'sewadar': What we know about Sukhbir Singh Badal's attacker
Sukhbir Singh Badal was attacked while he was walking towards the langar hall after paying obeisance at the gurdwara.
Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) president Sukhbir Singh Badal was attacked with a kirpan by a Nihang at Gurdwara Mata Sahib Kaur on the outskirts of Nanded Sahib in Maharashtra on Thursday.
Badal suffered an injury to his right hand and was shifted to a nearby hospital. He is now out of danger, HT has learnt.
READ ALSO | Ex-Punjab deputy CM Sukhbir Singh Badal attacked with 'kirpan' outside gurdwara in Maharashtra's Nanded
Who attacked Sukhbir Singh Badal?
The attacker was a Nihang dressed in blue attire and is reportedly in his mid-sixties. His identity has not yet been revealed. Security personnel accompanying Badal overpowered him and handed him over to the local police for questioning.
According to Jaimal Singh Dhillon, a functionary at Takht Nanded Sahib, the gurdwara is under the control of a Nihang Samparday and the attacker is said to be from Punjab.
The historic Nanded gurdwara is managed by a splinter group of Shiromani Panth Akali Budha Dal 96 Crori, a major Nihang organisation headed by Baba Maan Singh. The local jathedar is Baba Teja Singh. The accused Nihang was reportedly serving as a sewadar at the gurdwara.
Where was Sukhbir Singh Badal attacked?
The attack took place at Gurdwara Mata Sahib Kaur on the outskirts of Nanded, around 15 km from Takht Nanded Sahib, one of the five temporal seats of the Sikhs.
Badal was attacked while he was walking towards the langar hall after paying obeisance at the gurdwara. The shrine is controlled by a Nihang sect and is not managed by the board that oversees the main Nanded Sahib Gurdwara.
Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis sought details of the incident from the Nanded Superintendent of Police and directed authorities to investigate the motive behind the attack.
‘Attack on Punjab’s unity’: SAD leader
SAD national vice-president Sanjeev Talwar called the attack on party chief Badal a serious security lapse.
“Sukhbir Singh Badal is a promoter of Hindu-Sikh unity, he speaks of Punjab and Punabiyat,” Talwar said. “This is not a direct attack on Sukhbir Singh Badal but an attack on the unity and integrity of Punjab,” he added.
“Such attack on someone who has Z+ security and is a former Deputy CM will certainly be considered a security lapse,” he said.
Why was Sukhbir Badal in Nanded?
Badal reached Nanded on Wednesday with his family and a group of close associates for a three-day visit. He organised an Akhand Path at the gurdwara.
Earlier on Thursday, Badal was offered a siropa by the head priests at Sachkhand Nanded Sahib, the main gurdwara in Nanded and one of the five temporal seats of the Sikhs. Bathinda MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal and other family members were also present.
Gurdwara Mata Sahib Kaur is located around 15 km from the main Nanded Sahib gurdwara and is under the control of a Nihang Samparday.
Badal’s second attack in less than two years
The Nanded incident is the second attack on Sukhbir Badal in less than two years. On December 4, 2024, former militant Narain Singh Chaura allegedly attempted to assassinate Badal at the entrance of the Golden Temple in Amritsar.

“Heated Rivalry” actor Dylan Walsh has found himself on thin ice after revealing details about upcoming episodes in a video clip that has gone viral.
Walsh, who plays David Hollander on the hit hockey romance, recently paused his account on the celebrity video app Cameo after he got “in trouble” – in his words – for over-sharing in a clip about the upcoming second season of the series, which just began filming.

Popular on Variety

Sri Lanka’s southern coastal city stirred awake to the insistent whisper of rains at dawn. Water slanted down like sharp threads but once the clouds dissipated, the heat slithered in like a shroud that choked. As Thursday wore on, Shubman Gill’s men trained hard at the Galle International Stadium.
After the net session, India’s bowling coach Morne Morkel jogged a bit, and then faced the media. In the lead-up to the first Test against Sri Lanka from Saturday, questions ranged from team-composition to pitch-analysis.
India played a lone Test, the winning one against Afghanistan, earlier this year. Aware of this shortfall in cricket’s longest format, Morkel said: “We came 10 days earlier to give the guys the best opportunity to prepare. We haven’t played a lot of red-ball cricket and going back into that will be a challenge. We are quite excited to see how these guys can stand up and create pressure.”
On a surface expected to aid spin, Morkel did not deny the possibility of having three left-arm spinners ranging from the conventional Ravindra Jadeja and Manav Suthar to the unconventional Kuldeep Yadav, plying his chinaman wares. “Kuldeep is an attacking bowler, and with his experience and class we can’t look past. All three are different. One turns a bit more, and one is slightly more accurate. They have got the skill to get 20 wickets for us,” Morkel said.
The former South African speedster was not perturbed by the lack of experience in his pace attack: “All these guys have come a long way. Prasidh (Krishna) and (Mohammed) Siraj have played a lot of cricket back home, where it’s also tough bowling conditions. The biggest challenge will be the heat, the humidity, and the Kookaburra ball once it gets a little bit soft.”
Queried about the pitch, Morkel said: “It looks like a good surface and as the Test goes on, something will happen. We have prepared for all that can come our way. It’s more about the mental challenge now, facing these conditions, batting time, bowling those spells and getting the ball in the right areas.”
Reverse-swing was not ruled out too as Morkel explained: “It is definitely going to play a role. This morning we had quite a big shower, that will make the outfield a little softer and then it would take a bit longer for the ball to reverse. If you are a fast bowler, you will bowl short spells and you always will have an opportunity.”
Morkel was clear about the ideal strategy and it centred around excelling in the first innings and exerting pressure: “The first two days will belong to the batting side. Whatever happens at the toss, if you bat first make sure you go big and if you bowl first get the ball in the right areas.” Soon Morkel jogged away while the sun bathed the nearby Dutch fort and the Indian Ocean shimmered.

Supreme Court to test legality of Delhi Police's use of facial recognition of NEET protesters at Jantar Mantar
The Supreme Court will examine the legality of Delhi Police’s alleged facial recognition and biometric surveillance of Jantar Mantar protesters.
The Supreme Court on Thursday agreed to examine whether the Delhi Police’s use of facial recognition technology and biometric surveillance to monitor protesters at Jantar Mantar has legal backing, and whether such mass surveillance violates fundamental rights to privacy, dignity, free speech and peaceful assembly.
A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notice to the Centre and the Delhi Police commissioner on a public interest litigation filed by CPI(M) Rajya Sabha MP AA Rahim, challenging the alleged use of facial recognition technology, AI-powered surveillance systems and biometric identification tools against protesters.
Also read: 20 FIRs filed in Delhi over CJP protest violence
SC seeks Centre, Delhi Police response on surveillance
Senior advocate Menaka Guruswamy, appearing for Rahim, told the bench that the petition specifically challenged the use of facial recognition technology by the Delhi Police against protesters and alleged that the data collected was being held by private companies. “This is very specific prayer concerning facial recognition being used by the Delhi Police against protesters, and the data is held with private companies,” Guruswamy said.
Also Read: ‘Hands off our Jantar Mantar’: CJP reacts sharply to HC’s remarks on protest site
She said that the surveillance involved both a facial recognition vehicle and smart glasses, with data collected without the permission of those being monitored. “One maps your face and one is a vehicle. So spectacles are used and a vehicle is also used. And that data is all taken without permission. These private entities host the data. In violation, we will argue, of the DPDP Rules, CrPC and a variety of things,” she said.
The bench then directed that notice be issued and the plea be tagged with other pending petitions concerning the July 20 “Sansad Chalo” protest, which raise allegations of police excesses, including the use of pellet guns and violence against protesters and police personnel.
Also read: Biometric scanners in Delhi to be placed under CCTV watch
Plea alleges protesters subjected to biometric surveillance
The petition, filed through advocate Subhash Chandran KR, claims that since the commencement of the sit-in at Jantar Mantar on June 20, thousands of protesters, journalists and ordinary citizens have been subjected to “continuous and pervasive biometric surveillance”.
Rahim has sought a declaration that indiscriminate deployment of facial recognition and biometric surveillance against peaceful protesters is unconstitutional. He has also sought directions restraining the Delhi Police from deploying such technologies until Parliament enacts a law specifically authorising their use.
Also read: Police identify 2,873 protesters with ‘criminal backgrounds’
Petitioner seeks deletion of protesters’ biometric data
Among other reliefs, the petition seeks disclosure of the surveillance technologies, databases, standard operating procedures and vendor agreements used during the Jantar Mantar protest; deletion of protesters’ biometric data from NAFIS, CCTNS and allied databases; and a mechanism enabling individuals to ascertain whether their biometric information was collected and seek its deletion.
It has also sought directions to private vendors to permanently delete biometric information collected during the protest and certify such destruction, besides restraining them from using the data to train, develop or improve facial recognition or artificial intelligence systems.
According to the plea, the surveillance was carried out through CCTV cameras, drones, a Mobile Command and Control Vehicle and handheld devices, besides real-time facial recognition using the “Ikshana” surveillance vehicle and “AjnaLens” smart glasses. It also alleges collection of fingerprints through the NCRB’s “Abhigyan” application and their matching against the National Automated Fingerprint Identification System (NAFIS).
Plea questions legal basis for facial recognition at protests
The plea contends that there is no law authorising the biometric surveillance of people participating in a lawful protest. It argues that neither Delhi Police standing orders governing protests nor the Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022 permit such surveillance of peaceful demonstrators.
The petition relies on RTI responses obtained from the Delhi Police to claim that no privacy impact assessment was conducted before the surveillance was undertaken. It further alleges that an 80% similarity score is treated as a positive facial recognition match, despite the absence of any publicly available validation of the threshold.
It also claims that Delhi Police’s stated use of facial recognition technology is limited to tracing missing persons and identifying deceased persons, rather than policing peaceful assemblies.
Petition invokes privacy, free speech and assembly rights
The petitioner has invoked the Supreme Court’s 2017 privacy judgment in the KS Puttaswamy case, arguing that the alleged surveillance fails the constitutional requirements of legality, legitimate aim and proportionality. It contends that the indiscriminate deployment of facial recognition creates a chilling effect on the exercise of the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b), apart from being arbitrary and disproportionate under Article 14.
The plea also raises concerns over the retention and possible integration of the biometric information with national criminal databases, alleging that the data could be retained indefinitely without adequate statutory safeguards, purpose limitation or a defined retention policy.
Also read: ‘Jantar Mantar Season 2 going to start very soon’: CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke's big remark
Two private companies have also been made respondents to the PIL, Aditya Infotech Ltd, which allegedly supplied the “Ikshana” facial recognition vehicle, and Dimension NXG Pvt Ltd, which allegedly supplied the AjnaLens smart glasses. The plea alleges that the companies participated in the policing exercise and may continue to possess footage, facial templates and other biometric information of protesters. It also questions whether any data-processing or data-sharing agreements, or other contractual safeguards governing access to such sensitive information, were put in place.

Caution: Spoilers for "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" ahead.
With great power comes great responsibility — that's the iconic mantra that's been at the heart of Spider-Man since his introduction in 1962.
But in 2026, should that great power include the ability to run a mass surveillance program on the people of New York City, with nothing more than a quip to explain it?
If you go by the events of "Spider-Man: Brand New Day," in theaters now, in which Spider-Man (Tom Holland) uses illegal facial recognition technology to identify both Scorpion (Michael Mando), a criminal, and Jean Grey (Sadie Sink), a telepathic mutant running amok in NYC, the answer is yes.
The technology is remarkably similar to what Batman uses at the end of "The Dark Knight," released in 2008. Except in that film, using it was presented as a huge ethical dilemma, and it's ultimately destroyed.
It's been 18 years since "The Dark Knight." What does the treatment of surveillance in "Brand New Day" say about our attitudes toward it? They've changed.
Spider-Man's line 'speaks to the extreme extent to which people are surveilled right now'
Spider-Man reveals the technology when looking for Scorpion, telling Detective DeWolff (Liza Colón-Zayas) that he has "every camera in New York running a facial recognition scan."
"That sounds super illegal, Spider-Man," she responds. "I'm gonna pretend I didn't hear that."
He laughs and says it's "probably for the best."
Some Spider-Man fans were upset about Spidey's relaxed attitude toward the surveillance technology. On X and Reddit, they used nicknames like "Peter Thiel Parker" and "Palantir Parker" to describe the character.
Peter Thiel's Palantir Technologies provides government agencies, including ICE and the Department of Defense, with software such as Gotham. It "supports soldiers with an AI-powered kill chain" by integrating target identification and target effector pairing, among other capabilities, according to the company.
Nicholas Carnes, a political scientist, professor of public policy at Duke University, and co-editor of "The Politics of the Marvel Cinematic Universe," told Business Insider he was "very uncomfortable" with Spider-Man's illegal technology "being a throwaway line."
"I thought, my goodness, how blasé it seems to now say, 'Oh, I'm just going to do this. Don't tell on me, detective,'" Carnes said.
For Carnes, the nonchalance of the moment reflects how pervasive surveillance has become in our day-to-day lives. "That line can only exist in the movie in the way it does in a world where people are accustomed to being surveilled," he added.
The surveillance debate has shifted since 'The Dark Knight'
"The Dark Knight," released 18 years ago, approaches surveillance technology differently and shows just how far attitudes have shifted.
Bruce Wayne argues with his friend, Lucius Fox, about the implications of using surveillance tech on fellow citizens, leading Lucius to threaten to quit. The film climaxes with Bruce destroying the device, much to Lucius' relief.
The film was released in July 2008, near the end of George W. Bush's second term, when some Americans were concerned about the application of laws like the Patriot Act and the NSA spying on American citizens. A Gallup poll put Bush's approval rating at just 29% that summer.
Nearly two decades later, surveillance concerns haven't disappeared, but we've all gotten more accustomed to living with it in every part of our lives, including at home, at work, in our cars, and at school.
"Christian Bale was Batman in an era when people were getting really concerned about what's happening with their data. And Spider-Man is sort of surveilling the entire city in an era when people are being told a hundred times a day, 'AI is good, and it's your friend,'" Carnes said.
That's not to say "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" doesn't criticize government power. Carnes noted that the movie ultimately portrays government oversight in a negative light.
"This is a movie that really depicts a fictional department of the US government [the Department of Damage Control] as shadowy, abusive, unaccountable, and utterly immoral," Carnes said.
The film ends with Spider-Man breaking into a DODC facility and discovering the agency has been developing weapons specifically designed to take him down.
While Peter has regrets about creating technology that was used against Jean and could have catastrophic consequences for mutants in the future, he never reckons with becoming Big Brother himself.
Spider-Man's surveillance tech isn't so far removed from reality
The technology Spider-Man uses to fight crime — without any oversight — isn't unlike surveillance systems that are already in place today.
Automatic license plate readers (ALPRs), including those made by Flock Safety, are used by police departments across the country to search camera networks for vehicles of interest.
Proponents of the technology argue it could be a helpful tool in preventing crime, supporting victims, and aiding police work. Critics argue that the tech has accuracy problems, raises privacy concerns, and lacks reliable oversight.
For now, it seems Americans share critics' concerns. A March 2026 poll by the Center for Democracy and Technology found that 74% of respondents were "concerned about the privacy and security of their personal data that is held by the government."
That raises another question: whether seeing this kind of surveillance wielded casually by a trusted superhero — Spider-Man — can continue to normalize it.
But Carnes noted that audiences have accepted superheroes having technology that, in the real world, would not fly.
"We're OK with Spider-Man having that power because he's Peter Parker, and he's dear to us, and we trust him," he said. "We would not be OK with virtually anyone having that in the real world."

Millions crowd cities to see Spain's first total solar eclipse in over a century
MEDINACELI, Spain — Millions of people crowded cloudless cities and towns in Spain on Wednesday in search of the best views of a total solar eclipse, when the alignment of the sun, moon and Earth briefly plunged parts of the planet into darkness.
The crowds brought lawn chairs and umbrellas as they eagerly awaited the celestial spectacle, which began early in the evening. As the sky darkened, gradually at first and then quickly, people broke into applause and cheered. It was the country's first total solar eclipse in more than a century.
"It's simply impossible to imagine," Rosa Celiberti, a language teacher who watched from Medinaceli, a Roman-era hilltop town in northeast Spain, said with tears in her eyes. "No matter how many photos or videos you've seen, nothing comes even close to what it actually feels like."
Across a wide band of northern and central Spain and Portugal, millions of people enjoyed some of mainland Europe's best views of the eclipse. It also passed over slivers of Greenland and Iceland.
Totality — when the moon completely covers the sun's light — was expected to last less than 2½ minutes, reaching its maximum duration off Iceland's west coast. By the time it got to a small patch of Portugal and then to Spain, just before sunset, totality dwindled to a minute or so. The total eclipse then ended over the Mediterranean.
The eclipse was expected to draw at least a half-million additional visitors, Spanish authorities said. Demand for hotel rooms along the path of totality, including in the northern cities of A Coruña, Bilbao and Santiago de Compostela, soared.
Rural areas prepared for an influx of visitors
The event unfolded against the backdrop of scorching summer temperatures and wildfires, and Spanish officials rolled out a large public safety campaign.
Temperatures across much of Spain climbed above 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) in many areas where the eclipse was observed. Some 350 official viewing sites were set up across the sparsely populated interior, and more than 33,500 law enforcement officers were deployed to observation areas and access points, the Interior Ministry said.
Only weeks ago, the most destructive wildfire in Spanish history devoured 500 square kilometers (193 square miles) and forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people in Ávila, in central Spain. Several smaller wildfires remain active elsewhere in southern and central parts of the country.
Despite clouds, sky watchers in Iceland witnessed darkness
In Reykjavik, clouds did not prevent hundreds of people from gathering in bright raincoats in front of the landmark Hallgrímskirkja church as the skies darkened.
With rain falling, the disk of the sun was barely perceptible and then, suddenly, the lights went out. Only the glow of phones held aloft could be seen.
The crowd cheered the darkness as it rained harder and roared even louder when the first light returned. They did not wait to watch the remainder of the partial eclipse and quickly cleared out of the square.
Eclipse glasses sold fast
Special eclipse glasses were essential for safe viewing, even if only a sliver of the sun remained visible. The glasses are made with special filters that block solar radiation that can damage the eyes.
For months, supermarkets, department stores, museums and planetariums across Spain had sold or distributed the glasses, with many pharmacies running out of stock ahead of Wednesday.
On Tuesday evening in downtown Madrid, a long line formed outside a photo shop where a sign read, "We carry eclipse glasses."
One woman emerged triumphantly and reassured those waiting: "He has boxes and boxes of them!"
A ship circles waters near Greenland hoping to catch a glimpse
Sverre Rud, captain of the MS Spitsbergen, was circling the waters of Rypefjord in eastern Greenland trying to make sure he was perfectly positioned for his 126 passengers to view the spectacle. All day, people came up to Rud to ask if he had nailed the right spot, with no clouds.
"I will do my best," Rud said. "I will pull out my superman powers."
The eclipse may have been startling for the passengers, who had been experiencing 24 hours of daylight on a 17-day cruise in locations mostly north of the Arctic Circle.
Suddenly, for two minutes it was dark.
Even so, the mood on the polar ship had been pure anticipation.
"Everyone is very enthusiastic," Rud said. "When we were down for breakfast earlier, it was almost like a little bit of a Christmas Eve feeling here."
Hotel costs skyrocketed in Spain and Iceland
Rooms in Reykjavík, Iceland's capital, averaged more than $1,000 for Wednesday night as Icelanders prepared for their first total solar eclipse since 1954 and the first visible from the capital since 1433.
Prices were roughly double 2025 rates, according to data group Lighthouse Intelligence. Many tourists made bookings years in advance. But cloudy skies prevailed across much of the island.
Authorities expected up to 20,000 additional overseas visitors during an already busy peak tourist period. Iceland is home to fewer than 400,000 people.
The 70-room Hotel Keflavík in the Reykjanesbaer municipality was fully booked, with guests hoping to see around one minute and 45 seconds of totality.
"Eclipse time, of course, has been very demanding, and many people came to us early, like last year," said Steinþór Jónsson, the hotel's owner and manager.
Jónsson said he had seen nothing like it since 1986, the year the hotel opened, when U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev held a summit in Reykjavík.
"When I opened the hotel, we had Reagan and Gorbachev meeting. It was very hectic here," he said with a smile. "Besides Reagan and Gorbachev, the eclipse is the biggest."
Sun mostly obscured in Britain
Across Britain, where the sun was more than 90% obscured, people flocked to hilltop parks and anywhere with an open view of the sky to see the best eclipse since 1999.
In Greenwich Park, with views of the River Thames and central London, the sky turned an eerie gray as a sliver of light sat atop the moon like a hat.
Veronica Orozco popped open a bottle of champagne to share with neighbors as she witnessed the second eclipse of her life.
"I was in Venezuela and I was young and I thought that the sun would not come back. My dad said, 'It is science, of course it will come back,'" she recalled. "Now sitting here at the age of 41, it is still magical."
Aja Lilit, who turned 24 on Tuesday, said the eclipse was like a "birthday present from the universe."
She said the rare event made her think of how small she was at a "cosmic level."

A new survey in Arunachal Pradesh has documented recurring experiences of widespread harassment of members of the LGBTQIA+ community in the State.
Also read | On India’s rainbow trail | Queer-focused walks are finding an audience in the country
According to the Itanagar-based HimKai Research Institute (HRI), the pestering or provocation has led to identity concealment, discrimination-related distress, and low confidence in institutional protection among the LGBTQIA+ respondents in the State.
LGBTQIA+ expands to Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer or Questioning, Intersex, and Asexual.
The HRI conducted the anonymous online survey between June 2 and August 2. It received 62 submissions, one of which was excluded during geographic eligibility and data-quality screening because the self-reported home district could not be mapped in Arunachal Pradesh.
“Among the 61 respondents included in the analysis, 49.2% said they hid their gender identity or sexual orientation most of the time or always because of fear of discrimination or violence. Half of valid respondents said they felt accepted within their family rarely or never, while 44.3% said they felt safe in their local community rarely or never,” the HRI report said.
“Experiences of harassment and discrimination were reported across several settings. Some 91.8% of respondents reported verbal harassment at least rarely, while 52.5% reported physical threats or violence at least rarely. Among valid responses, 85.0% reported discrimination in school or college at least rarely, and 63.2% reported workplace discrimination,” it said.
The survey also found that 72.9% of valid respondents felt compelled to change their behaviour or appearance sometimes or more often to retain work or education. A further 57.9% said their identity affected access to employment or income opportunities at least rarely.
Religious, cultural exclusion
“Mental wellbeing emerged as a significant concern. Among valid responses, 76.7% reported experiencing stress, anxiety or emotional distress related to discrimination sometimes or more often, including 48.3% who experienced it most of the time or always. Access to mental-health or peer support was uneven: 41.0% said such support was available most of the time or always, while 36.1% said it was available rarely or never,” the report said.
The findings also point to a gap between awareness of rights and confidence in institutions. While 56.7% of valid respondents agreed that they were aware of their legal rights, 63.3% disagreed that laws and policies adequately protect LGBTQIA+ persons, and 66.7% disagreed that police and authorities respond sensitively to LGBTQIA+ issues.
Religion, culture and social belonging received particularly cautious assessments. Some 72.1% did not agree that religion or faith practices are accepting of LGBTQIA+ persons. More than half disagreed that their identity is compatible with their cultural or tribal background or that local traditions allow space for diverse identities, with 51.7% of valid respondents disagreeing that they feel a sense of belonging in society.
Healthcare emerged as a comparatively more positive area. Among valid respondents, 56.7% said that they felt comfortable accessing healthcare most of the time or always, and 75.0% said healthcare providers treated them with respect most of the time or always.
“Friends were the most frequently reported source of support, mentioned by 37 respondents, followed by LGBTQIA+ networks, mentioned by 12.
Six respondents mentioned. Awareness and sensitisation were the most common single priority identified for improving LGBTQIA+ lives in Arunachal Pradesh, followed by legal protection,” the report said.
HRI director Ranju Dodum said the study was intended to begin building locally grounded evidence on experiences that are often discussed without adequate data.
“LGBTQIA+ experiences in Arunachal Pradesh cannot simply be assumed from national conversations. Family, community, tribal identity, religion, education and employment all shape how people experience acceptance and safety here. This is a baseline study and its numbers must be read with methodological caution, but they point to questions that deserve deeper research and serious public discussion,” he said.
The report recommends sustained sensitisation programmes in schools, colleges, workplaces, healthcare institutions, police and public administration; confidential mechanisms for reporting discrimination; stronger mental-health and peer-support systems; safe community spaces; more inclusive education and workplace practices; and locally grounded engagement with families, community institutions and faith leaders.
The survey sample was predominantly young, with 90.2% of respondents between 18 and 35 years.

India, Indonesia launch project to restore 9th-century Prambanan Temple
India and Indonesia have launched a landmark project to restore the 9th-century Prambanan Temple, a UNESCO World Heritage Site near Yogyakarta.
India and Indonesia have launched a landmark project to restore the 9th-century Prambanan Temple near Yogyakarta, one of Southeast Asia’s most important Hindu heritage sites and a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its exquisite Ramayana sculptures.
The temple, which houses three grand shrines dedicated to Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, is also home to a famed Ramayana tradition that continues through its elaborate dance ballet performances.
This beautiful temple dates to the 9th century and is the second-largest Hindu temple in Southeast Asia, after the Angkor Wat Temple in Cambodia.
The Parmanand Temple (widely known as Prambanan) was originally built around 850 CE during the reign of King Rakai Pikatan of the Sanjaya Dynasty in Java, Indonesia. It was later expanded by subsequent kings and is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Ramayana Ballet at the Prambanan Temple is a spectacular traditional performance.
It brings the Hindu epic to life with over 200 professional dancers and gamelan musicians against the backdrop of the illuminated temples. The epic story is performed over 150 times every year and keeps the grand tradition alive.
The Prambanan Temple also has exquisite sculptural reliefs depicting the story of the Ramayana. In terms of the quality of the art, this is one of the finest depictions of the Ramayana story anywhere in the world.
(Benoy K Behl is a filmmaker, art historian and photographer who has taken over 53,000 photographs of Asian monuments and art heritage and made 146 documentaries. He is known for having documented the Ramayana tradition in 10 countries of South and Southeast Asia)

India's top carmakers have privately raised serious concerns about fuel contamination involving E20, petrol blended with 20% ethanol content. Despite public support, Maruti Suzuki, Tata Motors and Mahindra flagged worries privately, according to Reuters. Internal emails, reviewed by the agency, revealed these hidden concerns. The revelation comes after India's auto lobby withdrew a complaint related to E20 petrol. The Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM) submitted the letter on 28 July. SIAM withdrew it following the Centre's public assurance about E20 petrol. It claimed that certain figures in the letter needed further authentication. However, private industry emails showed no such data concerns existed, according to Reuters. Executives discussed the contamination findings internally without questioning their accuracy. E20 has been mandatory nationwide since 1 April this year. This rollout aims to reduce pollution and cut oil imports. Consumer complaints have grown regarding vehicle performance under this fuel. Many motorists report reduced mileage and increased wear on cars. Industry testing involved collecting over 250 fuel samples across India. These samples came from 21 states and territories nationwide. High chloride contamination emerged in samples from 18 states. High moisture content was also detected across multiple locations. Chloride levels reportedly reached up to 570 parts per million in Rajasthan. Delhi recorded levels up to 420 ppm in testing. Maharashtra showed readings as high as 357 ppm. India's permissible chloride limit currently stands at just 3 ppm. These findings, therefore, substantially exceeded official government standards. Moisture levels also breached permissible limits in several states. Andhra Pradesh recorded levels up to 13,000 ppm. Uttar Pradesh showed similarly high readings around 12,500 ppm. The government's moisture benchmark currently permits only 3,000 ppm maximum. Maruti's senior executive, Anoop Bhat, raised these concerns internally. He noted that fuel injectors could tolerate only 1 ppm chloride. Mahindra's engineer, R Ramaprabhu, warned about organic chloride. He said this contaminant caused rapid vehicle failures within 200km. He claimed most immediate post-fuelling failures stem from this contamination. Mahindra reportedly currently holds strong evidence supporting these findings. "Majority cases reported immediately after fuelling ... is due to organic chloride," Reuters quoted him as writing. SIAM told Reuters that the data was meant for internal discussion only. It said very few automakers had actually collected this data. The petroleum ministry didn't respond to Reuters' requests for comment regarding this issue. However, Minister Hardeep Singh Puri addressed concerns publicly last week. He said oil companies had started rigorous fuel testing before receiving SIAM's letter. Only four contamination cases were found during this testing process. State-run fuel retailers also conducted extensive testing recently, they said. They found no cause for alarm regarding fuel contamination concerns. Mahindra has since called email-based conclusions "completely baseless and incorrect". It insists testing remains limited and preliminary at this stage. Maruti and Tata did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment. Hydraulic pressure, autopilot disconnect: Turbulence-hit Air India Phuket-Delhi flight logged 9 warnings in a minute
Air India Phuket-Delhi flight: Warnings indicated low reservoir levels in the Yellow and Blue systems, autopilot disconnect and elevator flight-control fault.
A post-flight Centralised Fault Display System log from an Air India Phuket-Delhi flight that suddenly lost altitude and dropped 300 feet, leaving 24 people injured, revealed a series of warnings linked to the aircraft’s hydraulic systems, flight controls and autopilot.
The August 4 incident, which left 20 passengers and four crew members injured on flight AI2379, an Airbus A320 registered as VT-EXO, was classified as serious and led to an investigation by the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB).
The pilot’s initial post-flight drug screening was recorded as “non-negative”, meaning the sample had been flagged for further testing. His confirmatory test later returned positive for cannabis.
Multiple warning signs during aircraft plunge
Deep Dive
The log, seen by HT, shows nine warning messages appearing within a minute at 9.32am IST, when the aircraft had crossed the Odisha coast after flying over the Bay of Bengal.
The warnings indicated low pressure in the Green, Blue, and Yellow hydraulic systems, in various combinations. They also showed low reservoir levels in the Yellow and Blue systems, an autopilot disconnect and an elevator flight-control fault.
Notably, the aircraft’s hydraulic systems rely on pressurised fluid to transmit power and operate heavy mechanical components.
Two emergency-exit door sensor warnings were then recorded at 9.33am and 9.35am. No additional warnings involving the hydraulic systems or elevator were recorded for the following 43 minutes.
An engine anti-ice fault appeared at 10.16am, followed by another autopilot disconnect at 10.52am. Unlike the first disconnect, the second was not recorded alongside any hydraulic warnings. The log does not provide a reason for the disconnect.
The pressure readings changed across different system combinations within the same minute, rather than showing a single system failing and remaining in that state. This could indicate a temporary event, such as a sharp vertical movement or sudden loss of altitude. Such an event can briefly move fluid inside the hydraulic reservoirs, based on a reading of the log by HT against standard A320 fault-code references.
A sustained mechanical fault would likely have generated additional warnings, including messages indicating that the issue had recurred.
Flightradar24 data places the altitude change within the same minute as the cluster of warnings. The aircraft was flying at 36,160 feet when an altitude anomaly was recorded at 9.33am IST. It then descended to around 35,800 feet, representing a loss of about 360 feet, according to Flightradar data.
Pilot slept 30-35 minutes during flight
The pilot told investigators that he slept for 30 to 35 minutes during the flight, went to the washroom and then returned to stand behind the first officer, according to two people familiar with his account to the AAIB.
They said he was talking about the air conditioning system when the altitude event occurred and that he was thrown to the cockpit floor. The first officer was operating the aircraft, while the commander was acting as the pilot monitoring, the two people said.
A cabin crew member seated in the observer seat, which a departing pilot is required to assign when leaving the cockpit, helped the commander back up, the people said. This was the first detailed account from the cockpit crew about what happened aboard flight AI2379.
The complete sequence of events inside the cockpit could not be independently confirmed by the pilots' accounts to investigators.

Over the past few weeks, journalists, independent creators, news organisations, activists and Opposition politicians have been reporting a growing number of Instagram accounts being restricted in India or posts being arbitrarily taken down — many of them concerning the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, the brutal police crackdown that followed, or simply content critical of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government or its policies.
While the police arrested and detained protesters across cities, the government has simultaneously been taking down content on Instagram through notices that may have been issued under Section 79(3)(b) or Section 69A of the Information Technology (IT) Act. Yes, may have been, because there is no clarity to the entire mechanism whatsoever.
The Timing of the Censorship Frenzy
The timing of this state-sanctioned censorship frenzy is particularly alarming. It comes in the immediate aftermath of the CJP protests, a youth-led movement whose reach and mobilisation were powered overwhelmingly by the digital ecosystem, particularly Instagram. The platform played a pivotal role in transforming CJP from a satire page into a nationwide movement that forced the government to concede to some of its core demands.
Born as a reaction to a snide remark made by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, CJP found its nucleus in the social media spaces occupied by young people. The group created its Instagram page in early May, posting reels, memes and explainers and rapidly amassing a following that surpassed that of every major political party in India. With 26.5 million followers as of today, CJP demonstrated how online engagement could be converted into massive street mobilisation across the country.
From the 36-day sit-in and hunger strike by Sonam Wangchuk and protesting students, to the Jantar Mantar ‘Sansad Chalo’ march on July 20 and solidarity protests across cities, Instagram was the primary platform through which participants and the wider public received and disseminated information. It enabled volunteers, creators and ordinary users to amplify protest calls, coordinate demonstrations and broadcast events in real time.
Instagram, owned by Meta, was therefore not merely a digital record of the movement; it was one of the principal engines of it. The scale of the street mobilisation, catalysed by the platform, eventually forced the government to concede to several of CJP’s core demands, including former education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation, compensation for families of students who died by suicide, and several reformative measures announced by the government.
It is against this backdrop that the timing of the current censorship becomes especially significant. A platform that proved capable of turning youth discontent into one of the country’s largest grassroots movements is now at the centre of an opaque censorship drive, raising questions about what and who the state is seeking to silence.
Anti-establishment Wave Forces Modi to Make Reels
This digital upheaval also managed to create an unprecedented anti-establishment wave, which not only led to the resignation of a cabinet minister for the first time in BJP’s 12-year rule but also compelled Prime Minister Narendra Modi to create Instagram reels responding to the growing discontentment towards his governance.
The 75-year-old PM, who has not held a single press conference in 12 years, made five consecutive reels wherein he directly addressed the youth protesters — referring to them as ‘friends’ as opposed to his usual ‘Mitron’. A marked departure from BJP’s traditionally scripted social media communication, in his candidly-shot selfie videos, Modi assured the disgruntled Gen-Zs who steered the protest, that his government is committed to taking action against the paper leaks and is actively taking measures to resolve their grievances.
The entire censorship drive is playing out concurrently with tensions deepening between Meta and the BJP government, with many suspecting that the rise in censorship of anti-government content on Instagram is a result of the former succumbing to pressure.
The tech giant drew the government’s ire after it claimed to have erroneously removed Modi’s July 23 post addressing the protesting students from Facebook. Although the video was quickly restored, a parliamentary standing committee gave a three-day ultimatum to CEO Mark Zuckerberg to issue an apology while threatening to revoke the platform’s safe harbour immunity in India. This led to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan reportedly flying in from the United States, meeting Union minister Ashwini Vaishnav and apologising on behalf of the company on Wednesday.
‘Blanket Ban On Protest, Modi Related Content’
However, Modi’s ‘friendly assurances’ did not keep the government from suppressing dissenting voices on Instagram. On August 6, Thursday, CJP spokesperson Saurav Das shared screenshots on X of his Instagram posts being taken down, calling it a “blanket ban on protest and Modi related content”. The two posts, uploaded on June 12 and 18, were about Das’ arrival in Bengaluru for a peaceful protest and CJP securing police clearance for the July 20 protest in Delhi, respectively.

So Meta has restricted 4 of my videos in India.
One video showed how police was stopping food from reaching Jantar Mantar. The other was made when @Wangchuk66 was forcefully picked up.@Meta – I know this govt fears us, but last I checked, you were still preaching about free… pic.twitter.com/8wzVzxRr6r

CJP’s official Instagram page was briefly made unavailable in India on July 22, two days after the Jantar Mantar stir. “Cockroach Janta Party’s Instagram account has been taken down by Narendra Modi,” Dipke wrote on his X handle with the screenshot that displayed the message, “This is because we complied with a legal request to restrict this content.”
‘Automated’ Crackdown
Two videos uploaded by independent news outlet Maktoob Media on July 21 and 23 were blocked in India under the IT Rules. “Your post is unavailable in India. We restricted access to this content through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules,” the notification read.
View this post on Instagram
Speaking to Alt News, Maktoob Media editor Aslah Kayyalakkath said, “Both the videos were our original journalistic content analysing the protest and the subsequent police crackdown. The first video, in particular, examined how Right-wing propaganda media outlets were misrepresenting the protest. It was removed within minutes of being uploaded on July 21. Neither video contained graphic visuals, yet they were restricted without any specific explanation about what exactly violated the law.” He mentioned that the notification did not include any steps to appeal for withdrawing the restriction and mails to Meta did not yield any response.
“For an independent newsroom, this is not merely about two videos being unavailable. When documentation of protests and police action can disappear from a major platform without a clear reason, it raises serious questions about transparency, accountability and censorship,” he added.
Priyanshi Sharma, co-founder of independent news outlet Peek TV, posted on X that an August 4 interview with 23-year-old Shradha Singh, one of the protesters who allegedly received “rape and death threats”, was arbitrarily removed from their Instagram page. The video discussed the alleged harassment, doxxing and online abuse women protesters have been facing since July 20.

Sonal Hayat, a journalist with The Independent, told Alt News that her Instagram story on July 28, a repost of Hussain Haidry’s tweet on women criticising the BJP receiving “rape threats” by “BJP supporters and IT Cell”, was removed with the same notification citing “an automated system” and “IT rules”.
“I had just reshared a tweet adding that I had also been trolled by the IT Cell. I just got a notification that my story was removed, there was no reason given. This forms part of a pattern of the government just removing anything and everything that criticises them,” she said.
‘Anything Anti-Government Will Be Removed’
Political content creator Shrishti Khanna, who has been fighting an uphill battle with Instagram, told Alt News that her account with 104,000 followers was restricted in India, which compelled her to create a back-up account. “I have been creating political content on Instagram for a while, often discussing issues like the Palestinian genocide, local Indian politics, Hindutva, the RSS-BJP playbook. On June 9, my account, which had nearly 100,000 followers, was suddenly suspended without any prior notice within 24 hours of me posting about an alleged Israeli war criminal vacationing in India. Meta claimed it was due to copyright violations, even though the posts were entirely my own reporting. After I appealed, Meta admitted it was an error and restored my account,” she said.
“However, on July 7, my account was blocked in India by government order under Section 79(3)(b), which implies that it was intentionally flagged by a police officer and Meta had to comply. Again, I received no notice or mails from either Meta or the government. People started messaging me that they could not view my account in India. I opened my account and there was no notification. The whole process was so discreet that I only discovered the restriction by digging through Meta’s settings. My account was banned right after I spoke about Kashmir, but since no reason was communicated, this is just my hypothesis,” she said.

Khanna has approached the Delhi high court with a writ petition on the restriction and her next hearing is on September 2. “I have consistently been subjected to hate campaigns by Right-wing trolls, rape and death threats, and even AI-generated deepfakes of myself. If you say anything against the government or Modi, they will target you,” she said.
Content creator Anjali Priya told Alt News that on July 24 she received a notification that her July 23 satirical post demanding Pradhan’s resignation with a screenshot of Modi’s ‘Hi Friends’ video was restricted in India. “I was not given any prior notice that my post will be restricted in my own country where my entire audience base is. There was no reason except ‘we have received a legal request to restrict access to your post’ mentioned,” she said.
Three of Alt News co-founder Mohammed Zubair’s Instagram posts were restricted in India either citing the IT Rules or in accordance with Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. The posts, uploaded on May 19, June 8, and June 28, showed a youth recording himself voting eight times for a BJP candidate in Uttar Pradesh, BJP leader Nazia Elahi’s hate speech at a press conference, and skewed coverage of news agencies ANI, PTI & IANS, respectively.
In the same vein, news outlet Scroll.in on Thursday published a report stating that four of its Instagram posts were restricted in India, all similarly citing “legal requirements” under the IT Rules and “through an automated system”. The posts covered lack of compensation for Kashmir’s pellet gun victims, a photo showing pellet injuries, the contentious Chauhaan film teaser and a legal challenge to Amritsar’s meat-sale ban. All four, concerning politically sensitive issues and critical of government policy, were made unavailable in India without a specific reason. Scroll is yet to receive a response from Meta.
The Hindu on Friday also reported that their Instagram post on Kashmir pellet victim Insha Mushtaq was restricted in India. “The story on which the Instagram post was made was published on August 1 and we received a notice that it was restricted in India on August 8. The story is still up on our website, but we suspect that it has been restricted on Instagram. This is being done to deny the new generation access to politically sensitive stories, particularly stories on pellet guns, after it was reported that they were used during the CJP protests. This story also mentioned the CJP protests, and reportage on that is also being blocked on Instagram,” a source from The Hindu told Alt News.

Meanwhile, former chief minister of Delhi and Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) founder Arvind Kejriwal’s Instagram account was also momentarily restricted in India on Thursday.
He highlighted that lack of response from Meta on X, saying “… No one in your office is giving any reasons. No one is suggesting how restrictions can be removed. All emails written have elicited no response…Don’t bow down to our Prime Minister so much. Else he will allow u to run only his own account in India.”

Why have you restricted my account? Verbal enquiries at your India office revealed that my account has been restricted in India and is unavailable in India. Why? Noone in your office is giving any reasons. Noone is suggesting how restrictions can be removed.… pic.twitter.com/4JThAqFMon

AAP’s official handle on X also posted a screenshot of several Instagram posts being made unavailable in India. “No explanation. No accountability. Just silence…Meta, stop hiding behind silence. Tell India why accounts are being restricted on your platforms and whose orders you are acting on. Despite several emails, why are we still not getting a response?” read the post.
Vague Legal Orders and a Dead-end Appeals Process
This lack of transparency and any effective avenue for appeal against the takedowns trap users in a black box of opacity and confusion.
On August 6, the Union ministry of electronics & IT (MeitY) reiterated in a circular that the “timeline for the removal of unlawful content has been reduced from 36 hours to 3 hours”. The circular defines ‘unlawful content’ as “information prohibited under any law for the time being in force in relation to the interest of the sovereignty and integrity of India; security of the State; friendly relations with foreign States; public order; decency or morality; in relation to contempt of court; defamation; incitement an offence relating to the above; or any information which is prohibited under any law…” It is important to note that the amendments were notified as early as February, prior to the CJP protests.
The circular mandates ‘takedown notices’: “Social media intermediaries are required to remove any unlawful information as and when brought to their knowledge either through a court order or through a reasoned intimation, in writing from the Appropriate Government or its agency.” It also outlines a grievance redressal mechanism: “Intermediaries are required to appoint Grievance Officers and resolve complaints within the prescribed timelines. Users can appeal online at https://www.gac.gov.in if their complaints are not addressed by the intermediaries’ Grievance Officers.”
However, in several cases examined by Alt News, users highlighted that they received no prior notice or specific explanation for the restrictions. Meta’s notifications cited only two reasons: restriction in compliance with a legal request and through an automated system based on legal requirements under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. In most cases, users flagged how these notices were largely vague and lacked any real information on who ordered the restriction or what content allegedly violated the law. They also highlighted lack of an option to appeal for restoration of their accounts or posts, or response on mails sent to Meta directly.
Users said that upon clicking on the ‘See why’ after a post or account is restricted, the same message on automated systems and legal requirements under IT Rules appear and upon clicking ‘Where this happened’, ‘India’ appears as the location where the content is restricted. For ‘How we made this decision’, the exact same message that appeared in the initial notice, “We have taken this action based on a local legal requirement”, reappears; a very similar message is displayed upon opening Meta’s ‘Transparency Centre’ — creating a loop of opaque explanations. Below are the series of messages users encounter:
Affected users also the questioned the ‘automated system’ and and the lack of clarity over how it functions. “What is particularly shocking is Meta’s explanation. What exactly is this automated system? Does this mean there is now a system that automatically identifies and blocks journalistic content in the name of complying with legal requirements? The idea that this process could now be automated, without any transparency about why a particular piece of journalism is being blocked, is deeply alarming and dangerous for press freedom,” said Kayyalakkath.
As public discourse increasingly shifts from the streets to social media feeds, the rise in Instagram censorship begs the question: will there ever remain a space for democratic dissent in this country — online or offline?

Umesh Mehra had a fascinating conversation with Kiran Juneja on DD Urdu’s chat show Guftgoo about his memorable films and a lot more. He opened up about making Indo-Russian co-productions like Alibaba Aur 40 Chor (1980) and Sohni Mahiwal (1984) and shooting for these films in Russia.
Umesh Mehra reveals Sunny Deol’s TOUGH time shooting in Russia for Sohni Mahiwal as a vegetarian: “He survived on fruit, bread, butter, milk; NEVER complained”; recalls Hema Malini finding MEAT in her ‘vegetarian’ soup
Umesh Mehra said, “The biggest issue that Indians face in such countries is food! It was extremely cold aur hum logon ko bina garam khaane ke chalta nahin. Over there, the locals would usually eat bread, meat and cheese. We used to have fried eggs and bread. But it was so cold that by the time the fried egg went from the frying pan onto our plate, it would already be cold. And it’s no fun having thanda anda (laughs)! It was quite a torture. Later, we started flying our own cook in from India.”
He then talked about the Sohni Mahiwal leading actor, “For Sunny Deol, it was even more difficult as he was a vegetarian. He used to only have fruit, bread, butter and milk. That’s it. But hats off to him. He never complained about it.”

Umesh Mehra continued, “After some time, the soup was served. Hema ji was stirring it when she spotted a small piece of meat. Air India to screen all pilots for drug abuse after turbulent flight's captain found 'high'
Air India stressed the need to go beyond regulations prescribed by the DGCA “ to uphold the highest standards of safety and professionalism".
Air India on Thursday said all pilots will be screened for substance abuse before departures, days after the pilot-in-command (PIC) of a Phuket-Delhi flight that suddenly lost altitude last week tested positive for marijuana.
Twenty-four people, including four crew members, suffered injuries after the Phuket-Delhi AI2379 flight dropped 300 feet during cruise on August 4. An initial statement from Air India had cited turbulence as the reason. The PIC later tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test.
In an email to all its employees reviewed by HT, the Tata Group-owned airline stressed the need to go beyond the regulations prescribed by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) “ to uphold the highest standards of safety and professionalism, and to provide reassurance to our passengers, stakeholders and the community at large.”
“We have decided to undertake a full screening of all Group pilots for any substances or medications that are not permitted under prevailing regulations. This testing is mandatory and will start today, 13 August 2026,” the airline said.
“It will be conducted concurrent with training at the Gurugram Academy, post flight at our Flight Briefing Centres / Air India Offices, or at locations provided by your respective bases,” it added.
The airline said for decades, it has been the flag bearer of Indian aviation. “Over this time the professionalism, skill and commitment to safety of our pilots, together with other staff, has earned the trust of millions of passengers and the wider community. This trust is our most important asset, and it is vital that we do all possible to protect and sustain it. Many of you have recently reached out to share the same sentiment,” it said.
“As you know, Air India already fully complies with all regulatory requirements prescribed by India’s DGCA, which are similar to those practiced in other major aviation jurisdictions including Europe and the United States. We nevertheless now feel that it is important to go further,” it added.

Hodgkinson into 800m final after dramatic Werro fall
- Published
Keely Hodgkinson's bid for European gold continued as she stormed into the final of the women's 800m - moments after rival Audrey Werro suffered a dramatic fall that put her place in Friday's showpiece in doubt.
Werro - who ran the fastest time for 43 years earlier this season - led from the start in the first semi-final, but crashed to the floor on the final bend.
The Swiss 22-year-old got back to her feet a moment later and finished the race in last place, grimacing and clutching her chest.
However, Werro will race against Hodgkinson in a highly anticipated final following a successful appeal, with footage showing France's Anais Bourgoin had hit Werro's right foot with her left hand.
An earlier angle seemed to show Werro had clipped her own leg before falling.
There was less drama in the second semi-final, with Hodgkinson safely crossing the line first in one minute 57.38 seconds.
The Olympic champion led from the start and held off the fast-improving Femke Broeders-Bol - a two-time world 400m hurdles champion who chose to switch events this season - to advance.
Asked if she had seen Werro's fall before her race, Hodgkinson told BBC TV: "I heard an 'ooh' [from the crowd] which is never a good sign. I don't know what it looked like."
Speaking before Werro's appeal, Hodgkinson added: "Obviously it's a real shame and I hope she's OK.
"I hope she's in the final tomorrow [Friday], that'd be a really exciting race."
The women's 800m has become the must-watch event of the championships because of the expected three-way battle between Hodgkinson, Werro and Broeders-Bol.
"The excitement makes me excited. I can't wait to step out there. It brings out the best in me," Hodgkinson added.
"I love a good challenge. Hopefully it'll be a good race, a clean race, nobody falling over."
Hodgkinson will be joined in the final by fellow Briton Jemma Reekie, who capitalised on Werro's fall to win the first semi-final.
There will be 10 athletes in Friday's final instead of nine, with Lithuanian athlete Gabija Galvydyte - who was clipped by Werro as she fell - also advancing alongside the Swiss.

Telangana school principal found dead with 27 stab wounds at her home: Police
Kallu Roopa Reddy, principal and director of Nagarjuna Grammar English Medium School in Kondamallepally, suffered around 27 stab wounds in the attack
A 48-year-old school principal was stabbed to death by unidentified people at her residence in Telangana’s Nalgonda district on Wednesday, police said, suspecting that people known to the victim could be behind the murder.
Kallu Roopa Reddy, principal and director of Nagarjuna Grammar English Medium School in Kondamallepally, suffered around 27 stab wounds in the attack. Police said no cash or valuables were missing from the house, ruling out theft as an apparent motive at this stage.
“She lived with her husband, Kallu Rajender Reddy, at their own house in the Colony. The couple also owned a house in Hyderabad, where their son Abhinav Reddy was pursuing engineering, and they frequently travelled between the two places,” Devarakonda deputy superintendent of police M V Srinivas Rao said.
According to the police, Roopa Reddy had gone to Hyderabad with her husband on a three-day holiday on Saturday. As Rajender Reddy had some work in Hyderabad, she returned alone to Kondamallepally on Tuesday morning and attended school.
“She remained at the school until around 5.30 pm and returned home, which is closer to the school, telling her colleagues that some friends were expected to visit her. However, she did not come to the school on Wednesday and when her husband called her, he could not reach her,” Rao said.
He then contacted tenants staying in their house and asked them to check on his wife, but they also received no response.
Rajender contacted Chintapalli sub-inspector Rammurthy, who lives next to their house, and requested him to check the residence. The SI, accompanied by neighbours, went to the house and found Roopa lying in a pool of blood.
Police subsequently examined the premises with a dog squad. “The victim had suffered about 27 stab wounds, indicating the brutality of the attack. No cash or valuables were missing from the house, ruling out theft as an apparent motive at this stage,” Rao said.
The police are examining the possibility that persons familiar with Roopa may have committed the murder. Family disputes and other possible motives are also being investigated.
A case was registered based on a complaint lodged by the victim’s son, Abhinav Reddy, and further investigation is under way, Rao said.

Excise policy: Arvind Kejriwal, Manish Sisodia move Delhi HC to dismiss CBI’s appeal
Kejriwal and Sisodia argued that the agency filed the appeal with “unprecedented haste” and in a manner that reflected a lack of seriousness
Former Delhi chief minister (CM) Arvind Kejriwal and ex-deputy CM Manish Sisodia have moved the Delhi high court seeking dismissal of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI’s) appeal challenging trial court’s order discharging them in the excise policy case.
In their application filed on Wednesday, days before the high court scheduled hearing CBI arguments on August 17, Kejriwal and Sisodia argued that the agency filed the appeal with “unprecedented haste” and in a manner that reflected a lack of seriousness.
They contended that the appeal was filed within four hours of the trial court’s discharge order, which runs into more than 500 pages.
According to the two leaders, the speed with which the CBI preferred the appeal “manifestly shows” that the agency could not have properly appreciated or considered the detailed findings and reasoning contained in the discharge judgment.

“That the entire Revision Petition is sans pointing out any specific finding/paragraphs of the discharge order which according to CBI show the perversity. Hence the present Petition fails the test of a Revision Petition being filed under Section 442 BNSS. The present Petition is nothing but an Appeal which is filed in garb of the Revision Petition,” the application stated.
It further submitted that the CBI’s petition fails to make specific allegations against each accused, including how the discharge order was passed without evidence, what material evidence was allegedly ignored in relation to a particular accused or which specific finding, paragraph in the judgment reflects an arbitrary or perverse exercise of judicial discretion.
“The CBI has also failed to produce any evidence, materials or documents with the present revision petition to show the perversity in the order of discharge. The present petition is incomplete as it is without the material being relied upon and the specific averments in the order of discharge and hence it is liable to be dismissed in the present form,” the application added.
On February 27, the trial court discharged Kejriwal, Sisodia and 21 others, holding that the CBI’s material did not even disclose a prima facie case, prompting the agency to challenge the order before the HC.

Kejriwal, Sisodia urge Delhi HC to dismiss CBI plea in liquor policy case
AAP leaders Arvind Kejriwal and Manish Sisodia have asked the Delhi High Court to dismiss the CBI's revision plea in the liquor policy case. Their response sharpens the legal battle over whether the agency can overturn the trial court's sweeping discharge order.
AAP leaders Arvind Kejriwal and Manish Sisodia on Monday asked the Delhi High Court to dismiss the CBI's petition against their discharge in the liquor policy case, saying the agency moved with "unprecedented haste" and in the "most unserious manner".
In separate applications, the former Delhi Chief Minister and his former deputy questioned whether the CBI's revision petition could be entertained at all. They said the plea was a "bare-shell" and "non-specific" petition and that they had been unable to understand the agency's case against them from what it had filed.
"The CBI has preferred the present revision petition with unprecedented haste and in the most unserious manner. The present revision petition was filed only within four hours of passing of the order of discharge by the Ld. Special Judge, which manifestly shows non-appreciation of the findings of the Ld Special Judge in the discharge judgement running into more than 500 pages," the application stated.
"Thus, if such a petition is held to be maintainable, a grave prejudice will be caused to the respondent herein," it added.
Justice Manoj Jain is scheduled to hear the CBI's petition, which challenges the trial court's February 27 order, on August 17 and 18. On the previous occasion, the judge had given Kejriwal, Sisodia and Durgesh Pathak a final opportunity to file their replies within two weeks.
In their latest applications, Kejriwal and Sisodia said the trial court had discharged all the accused after hearing the matter in detail for more than three months, but the CBI had not pointed to any specific finding that was "perverse" or showed any irregularity. They said the agency had only listed "self-serving facts" and had not explained how the discharge of each accused was ordered without considering the evidence.
"The present petition is incomplete as it is without the material being relied upon and the specific averments in the order of discharge -- hence it is liable to be dismissed in its present form. It is clear from the present petition filed by the CBI that not a single paragraph out of 1133 paragraphs of the discharge judgment is referred by CBI to suggest the perversity in the order," the application stated.
Kejriwal and Sisodia also said the High Court's powers in such a case were limited and had to be used cautiously, only where there was grave perversity.
"The revision petition seeks to re-narrating and re-examination of evidence. This is being stated solely for the reason that the Revisionist/CBI has failed to plead any such specific instances, hence, it cannot assume that this Hon'ble Court would re-appreciate/re-examine the entire evidence on record. The said exercise cannot be done in the Revisional Jurisdiction," the application stated.
On February 27, the trial court discharged Kejriwal, Sisodia and 21 others in the liquor policy case, saying the case was wholly unable to survive judicial scrutiny and stood discredited in its entirety. In its revision petition, the CBI has said the discharge order was patently illegal, perverse and showed errors on the face of the record.
The agency has argued that the trial court conducted a "mini-trial" at the stage of framing charges, relied on a "selective reading of the prosecution case", failed to appreciate the facts, and made unwarranted adverse remarks against the investigating agency and the investigating officer.
The matter will now come up before the high court on August 17 and 18, with the CBI pressing its challenge to the discharge order and Kejriwal and Sisodia seeking dismissal of the agency's petition.
